excerpt: From Chamorro proas in the Marianas to childhood river crossings in Luzon, a personal essay on cultural memory and the rediscovery of the Filipino balangay.
author: Lexi Zotomayor
bodyText:
My ten years in the Marianas were an odyssey of self-discovery. Living alone, far from home, tested the limits of my patience and nerve. Yet unlike Odysseus, whom the gods punished for the trick of the Trojan horse, I chose my journey, and found those years away to be an unexpected blessing.

During that decade in the archipelago, I had plenty of time to take stock of myself and of the islands around me. The Chamorros and Carolinians carry a deep, living pride in their maritime past. They speak of their *proas*, the swift outrigger canoes that carried their ancestors across open ocean to settle remote specks of land, as though the voyages happened yesterday. Watching them made me think of my own *kababayans*, and how little we celebrate our *balangays*.

I suppose we have an excuse. We are a nation scattered across more than seven thousand islands, divided into small kingdoms and sultanates long before Western ships arrived.

Most of us in the north never felt the pull of the *balangay* the way the Butuanons or the people of the Visayas do. The philosopher Paul Ricoeur wrote that memory is rooted in lived experience. It shapes who we are, alone and together, and binds a community to its past.

My own childhood memory of boats is modest. The only vessel I knew was the wooden *banca*, pushed along by bamboo poles on either side, that ferried ten passengers at a time across the river to my grandparents' house. The trip took less than five minutes and cost twenty-five centavos. Even then, the river was already dying. It ran moss green on clear days, and turned a muddy brown after a storm washed soil down from the hills.

So when I read about *balangays* in grade-school textbooks, the words meant nothing to me. My elders had no stories to tell about those ancient planked boats from the south. The Butuanons, by contrast, hold a cultural memory vivid enough to rival that of the Chamorros. Archaeology shows their ancestors built sturdy vessels that plied the southern inter-island routes and crossed the South China Sea.

Even after the old boatbuilding died out, the people of Butuan kept the story alive, passing their lived experience down from parent to child.

I did not grow up with that inheritance. Few of us in Luzon did. For years, a boat to me meant only a pair of bamboo poles dipping into green river water for twenty-five centavos. Only recently has the *balangay* stopped being a flat sketch on a textbook page. Archaeologists in Butuan have preserved the ancient planks and rebuilt the vessels on computer screens and in full-sized wood, introducing a new generation to the craft of their ancestors. The *balangay* has finally left the page and returned to the water, where it belongs.
title: The Forgotten Balangays
